facts.fact_text: The present case primarily concerns the applicant's complaint that his arrest at a demonstration had amounted to an interference with his rights to freedom of expression and freedom of assembly, in breach of Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention.
On 29 November 2019 a demonstration was held in front of the National Parliamentary Library of Georgia.

The demonstration on 29 November 2019 was part of a series of protests about the Parliament of Georgia's failure to adopt amendments to the Constitution of Georgia meant to facilitate the transition of the parliamentary electoral system from a 'mixed-member' system to one of proportional representation (see Makarashvili and Others v. Georgia, nos. 23158/20 and 2 others, §§ 5-6, 1 September 2022).
The demonstration on 29 November 2019 was attended by opposition politicians, civil society activists and ordinary citizens.
Video material relating to the demonstration on 29 November 2019 shows a couple of hundred individuals gathered at the site.

Video coverage of the demonstration on 29 November 2019 shows that the demonstrators attempted several times to break through the police cordon and force their way to the entrance of the National Parliamentary Library of Georgia while the Minister of Justice was there.

Video coverage of the demonstration on 29 November 2019 shows that the pavement and narrow road leading to the entrance of the National Parliamentary Library of Georgia were largely occupied by people who had gathered at the demonstration, including police officers.
Six individuals, including the applicant, were arrested on 29 November 2019 on various grounds.

At some point during the demonstration on 29 November 2019, the applicant turned towards the police officers, allegedly in response to the police calls to clear the road, holding beans in his hand and shouting loudly that beans used to be 'gruel for slaves'.
According to the case file, the applicant then threw the beans at the police officers, crying out 'slave gruel for the police'.

The present case primarily concerns the applicant's complaint that his arrest at a demonstration had amounted to an interference with his rights to freedom of expression and freedom of assembly, in breach of Articles 10 and 11 of the Convention.
Six individuals, including the applicant, were arrested on 29 November 2019 on various grounds.
The applicant was escorted to the Tbilisi police station for having allegedly committed offences under Article 166 of the Code of Administrative Offences (disorderly conduct/minor hooliganism).

The applicant was escorted to the Tbilisi police station for having allegedly committed offences under Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences (disobeying lawful orders of a law-enforcement officer/insulting a law-enforcement officer).

On 29 November 2019 the Tbilisi City Court found the applicant guilty of insulting law-enforcement officers and disobeying their lawful orders, in breach of Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences.
The Tbilisi City Court sentenced the applicant to eight days' administrative detention.
The administrative-arrest report indicated Articles 166 and 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences as the provisions relevant to the applicant's arrest.

Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences, as worded at the material time, provided that 'disobeying a lawful instruction or order issued by a law-enforcement officer on duty or insulting the latter' was punishable by a fine of a minimum of 1,000 Georgian laris and a maximum of 4,000 Georgian laris, or up to fifteen days' administrative detention.
The Tbilisi City Court noted that section 48(3) of the Police Act provides that insulting the honour and dignity of police officers who are on duty will incur liability under Georgian legislation.

The Tbilisi City Court noted that Article 173 of the Code of Administrative Offences expressly defines liability for disobeying the lawful orders of police officers on duty, verbally insulting them and/or carrying out insulting actions towards them.

The Tbilisi City Court noted that on 29 November 2019 a demonstration was being held along the site of the public library in Tbilisi, on Purtseladze Street, and that police officers were ensuring the peaceful conduct of the demonstration and the implementation of the constitutionally guaranteed rights of citizens.

The Tbilisi City Court found that the police officers were enforcing security, protecting the rights of the participants in the demonstration and ensuring citizens' constitutionally guaranteed right to freely move along Rustaveli Avenue and the adjacent streets, which constituted sufficient grounds for the officers to implement appropriate measures provided for by law.

The Tbilisi City Court found that the law-enforcement authorities gave instructions to preserve order and that the instructions were lawful and aimed at achieving the legitimate goal of safeguarding individuals and public order.

Video coverage of the demonstration on 29 November 2019 shows that the demonstrators attempted several times to break through the police cordon and force their way to the entrance of the National Parliamentary Library of Georgia while the Minister of Justice was there.

At some point during the demonstration on 29 November 2019, the applicant turned towards the police officers, allegedly in response to the police calls to clear the road, holding beans in his hand and shouting loudly that beans used to be 'gruel for slaves'.
According to the case file, the applicant then threw the beans at the police officers, crying out 'slave gruel for the police'.

The Tbilisi City Court considered that actions insulting the dignity of police officers — calling them 'slaves' and throwing beans at them while noting that beans used to be gruel for slaves — cannot be considered a form of protest.

The Tbilisi City Court found that a need to block the road had not been demonstrated in the present case and accordingly the applicant did not have a right to occupy it, and the police officers' repeated requests to have the road cleared to allow cars to circulate were lawful but not complied with.
